annotations.text:
WHY THIS EXISTS (29 OCTOBER 2026)

The watcher (watch/, PR #30) checks every service we run once a minute, mails the operator when one stops answering, and sends the week in numbers on Monday mornings. Between Mondays, the only way to see a number is a database query in a terminal.

This is the page to look at in between: is everything up, how the relay is doing, and whether people are finding the site. It's for the maker, not a household, so nothing here is product wording, and it is never linked from the site or the panel.

TODAY: A PLAIN-TEXT MAIL ONCE A WEEK

The Monday note is complete and honest, and it's all there is. It arrives once a week and can't be asked anything in between. It has no shape: a rising week and a falling week look the same until the numbers are read one by one. A Down mail says something broke, but nothing shows what the rest of the week looked like around it.

The note stays whichever direction is picked. The page is for the days between notes, and for looking back.

A: THE ANSWER FIRST

The first thing on the page is the one question you open it to ask: is everything up? A sentence answers it, in the words the mail would use. Below it, every service gets a row: up now, its last seven days as a strip of four-hour marks where a miss is the one red mark, the week's uptime, and how fast 95 answers in 100 came back. The week's four numbers sit to the right, with the relay's disk, memory and load beneath them.

The case: it's the page you open when a mail has said Down, and the page you glance at when nothing has. A real outage changes the sentence and turns that row's mark red, and nothing else moves. It's a status page first and a growth page second, which is the right order for a service households pay for.

B: THE WEEK FIRST

The services shrink to one line across the top: all 9 up, the week's uptime, and the one outage. That line becomes a red band naming the service when something is down. The page leads with what's changing: page loads by week, eight weeks with this one lit, which pages they were, and four numbers along the bottom.

The case: uptime is the mail's job, and it already does it well, so the page is for the question the mail answers badly, which is whether the hub is growing. It costs A's per-service week: you see an outage only as a line, and the detail is a click away.

C: ONE LINE OF TIME

Every measure gets its own lane on one shared time axis, thirty days by default: page loads a day, joins a day, houses dialed in, any outage, and the relay's disk against the 85% line where the watcher writes. Each lane has its own scale, so nothing pretends two measures share an axis. Hovering a day reads every lane at once.

The case: the useful question is usually why. Monday's spike in page loads sits directly above Monday's three waitlist joins, which is the post that brought them. Tuesday's outage sits under a quiet night. A and B show each number on its own; C shows them together. It's the hardest of the three to read at a glance: a glance tells you less about whether everything is up right now.

BEHIND ANY OF THEM

The page is served by the watcher itself, which already holds every number: its own database, the site's counts and the waitlist. It adds no server and no new company. It's kept private by Cloudflare Access, on the account the site is already on, with a one-time code sent to the operator's mailbox. It's made in watch/terraform like the rest. Nothing on it is a visitor's or a house's: counts only, the same as the mail.

TO PICK

A, B or C, or a mix (B's chart under A's rows, say), or something else entirely: describe it. Whichever wins is built in watch/worker.js and pinned by a test, and the other two stay here with their cases.
